title: Reynolds-number-dependent entrance bias in temperature polarization of lab-scale membrane distillation
authors: Soyoung Kim, Tiezheng Tong, Yinuo Noah Yao
abstract: Lab-scale membrane distillation (MD) modules are commonly used for membrane characterization and developing empirical heat-transfer correlations. Entrance-induced flow structures can introduce geometry-specific effects into measured temperature polarization (TP) and heat transfer. However, the dependence of these effects on module geometry and flow condition remains unclear. We performed three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of direct contact membrane distillation (DCMD) over inlet Reynolds numbers of $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}=10$-$1000$, focusing on side-chamber length and main-channel height. We discovered that counter-rotating streamwise vortices formed near the main-channel entrance across all geometries, but their downstream persistence increased with $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$. At lower $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$, the vortices mostly decayed before mid-channel, while at higher $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$ they persisted farther downstream and produced pronounced spatial variations in TP. Increasing side-chamber length reduced the secondary-flow kinetic energy entering the main channel, and generally strengthened TP, whereas increasing main-channel height reduced the bulk velocity and streamwise kinetic energy, resulting in a thicker thermal boundary layer and stronger TP. For most geometries, the deviation from the straight-channel baseline changed from stronger TP at lower $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$ to weaker TP at higher $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$. Entrance effects therefore vary in both magnitude and direction with operating condition and cannot be represented by a constant correction across the Reynolds-number range.

infographic.key_insight: Entrance-induced vortices create geometry-dependent temperature-polarization bias whose magnitude and direction change with inlet Reynolds number.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Lab-scale membrane characterization and heat-transfer correlations should account for inlet geometry and operating conditions rather than use a constant entrance correction.
method: Performed 3D CFD simulations of direct contact membrane distillation.
Varied inlet Reynolds number from 10 to 1000, side-chamber length, and main-channel height.
Compared temperature polarization with a straight-channel baseline.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across all simulated geometries, entrance vortices formed and persisted farther downstream at higher Reynolds numbers; most geometries shifted from stronger polarization than the baseline at low Reynolds numbers to weaker polarization at high Reynolds numbers.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports simulation results but no experimental validation, so transfer to physical modules requires verification.
infographic.paper_title: Reynolds-number-dependent entrance bias in temperature polarization of lab-scale membrane distillation

title: Fourier-Feature-Embedded Complex-Valued Physics-Informed Convolutional Residual Networks for Sparse and Gappy Noisy Flow-Field Reconstruction
authors: Biswanath Barman, Rajendra K. Ray
abstract: Reconstructing flow fields from sparse and noisy measurements becomes particularly challenging when data are completely absent from dynamically critical regions, such as the vortex-formation region of a wake. Conventional interpolation and numerical reconstruction methods generally require sufficient spatial or boundary information, while physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can also face difficulties when sparse and noisy observations provide little or no supervision in the region of interest. To address this gap, we propose a Fourier-feature-embedded complex-valued physics-informed convolutional residual network (FCV-PICRN) for sparse, gappy, and noisy flow-field reconstruction. The framework integrates Fourier features for oscillatory and multiscale structures, complex-valued representations for coupled amplitude--phase learning, and convolutional residual blocks constrained by the Navier--Stokes equations. The method is first verified using the Taylor--Green vortex at $Re=100$ and then evaluated for the cylinder wake at $Re=100$. Three severe missing-data configurations are imposed in the dynamically sensitive wake: a large hole, a large truncation, and a plus-shaped gap extending in both streamwise and transverse directions. These gaps are further combined with additive Gaussian and multiplicative speckle noise. Despite having no supervised velocity data inside the excluded regions, FCV-PICRN reconstructs velocity, pressure, and vorticity with high structural similarity index (SSIM) and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), and remains robust under Gaussian noise up to $20\%$. Finally, for forced two-dimensional Kolmogorov turbulence with $5\%$ Gaussian noise, FCV-PICRN yields lower reconstruction errors than a conventional PINN. These results demonstrate robust physics-informed reconstruction of severely incomplete and noisy flows across laminar and turbulent regimes.

infographic.key_insight: FCV-PICRN reconstructs flow structures across large unsupervised gaps by combining Fourier features, complex-valued learning, and Navier–Stokes constraints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support flow diagnostics when sensors or imaging leave critical wake regions unobserved or noisy.
method: Fourier features encode oscillatory and multiscale flow structures.
Complex-valued convolutional residual blocks learn coupled amplitude–phase representations.
Navier–Stokes constraints guide reconstruction of velocity, pressure, and vorticity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests cover Taylor–Green and cylinder-wake flows at Re=100, three severe gap geometries with Gaussian or speckle noise, robustness to 20% Gaussian noise, and lower errors than a conventional PINN on 2D Kolmogorov turbulence with 5% Gaussian noise.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to the reported benchmarks; performance on three-dimensional, higher-Reynolds-number flows remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Fourier-Feature-Embedded Complex-Valued Physics-Informed Convolutional Residual Networks for Sparse and Gappy Noisy Flow-Field Reconstruction

title: Influence of Droplet Morphology on Fluid Dynamics and Impact Erosion of Wind Turbine Blades
authors: Hao Hao, Antonis Sergis, Maria N. Charalambides, Alex M. K. P. Taylor, Yannis Hardalupas
abstract: The impact of droplets, such as rain and sea sprays, on wind turbine blade surfaces can cause severe damage through leading-edge erosion (LEE). Current industrial practice has largely relied on empirical fatigue models to predict damage progression and guide maintenance. However, an important limitation of existing models is the assumption on ideal impact conditions, including perfectly spherical droplet and normal incidence, which rarely occur in reality. This study develops a fluid-structure interaction (FSI) model that couples incompressible multiphase flow simulations with finite element (FE) analysis of blade materials. Using this framework, we investigate the impact dynamics of droplets with arbitrary shapes and orientations. The results reveal a positive correlation between the peak impact pressure, the influential area at the pressure peak, and the peak impact force. In contrast, the time of peak force scales inversely due to momentum conservation. From these findings, we propose a $\textit{universal scaling law}$ that relates all key impact loadings to the simple parameter of the droplet $\textit{projection area}$, which can be determined solely from the initial droplet geometry and orientation. This law provides a predictive framework for impact loading dynamics of non-ideal shapes, offering new insights into the mechanisms of LEE and improving the accuracy of erosion predictions for wind turbine blades.

infographic.key_insight: Droplet projection area provides a geometry-based scaling parameter for predicting impact loads from droplets with non-ideal shapes and orientations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accounting for droplet morphology could improve wind turbine leading-edge erosion predictions beyond idealized spherical, normal-incidence impacts.
method: Couple incompressible multiphase flow simulations with finite element analysis of blade materials.
Investigate impact dynamics across arbitrary droplet shapes and orientations.
Derive a universal scaling law using initial droplet projection area.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations show positive correlations among peak pressure, influential area at the pressure peak, and peak force, with peak-force timing scaling inversely; the abstract reports no quantitative errors or experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: The proposed scaling law needs validation across realistic rain conditions and blade materials before use in erosion-life predictions.
infographic.paper_title: Influence of Droplet Morphology on Fluid Dynamics and Impact Erosion of Wind Turbine Blades

title: A GENERIC-Informed Neural Network for Generative Rheology
authors: Imanol García de Beristain, David Nieto Simavilla, Marco Ellero
abstract: We present GINNGER (GENERIC-Informed Neural Network for GEnerative Rheology), a framework for discovering thermodynamically admissible constitutive equations from microstructural flow data. Unlike existing approaches that learn constitutive operators, GINNGER reformulates constitutive discovery as the learning of the underlying thermodynamic generators from which constitutive equations emerge. Embedding the GENERIC formalism into the learning process restricts the search to constitutive models that satisfy the first and second laws of thermodynamics by construction, eliminating the need to prescribe phenomenological constitutive equations a priori. A second conceptual advance is a spectral formulation of constitutive discovery in the intrinsic eigenspace of the polymer conformation tensor. This provides a kinematics-independent thermodynamic state space in which the thermodynamic generators depend only on the instantaneous microstructural state, while flow kinematics acts solely as an external driver transporting the system through this space. Consequently, data from shear, extensional, and mixed flows contribute to the discovery of a single constitutive model that generalizes across deformation protocols and flow geometries. By learning thermodynamic generators rather than high-dimensional constitutive operators, GINNGER substantially reduces the complexity of the discovery problem while preserving thermodynamic consistency, material objectivity, and physical interpretability by construction. The framework is validated using high-fidelity simulations, accurately reconstructing constitutive behavior and predicting complex flow fields across previously unseen geometries. GINNGER establishes a new paradigm for constitutive discovery by combining generative, spectral, and thermodynamically grounded learning within a unified framework for data-driven modeling of complex fluids.

infographic.key_insight: GINNGER learns thermodynamic generators rather than constitutive operators, yielding rheological models that obey the first and second laws of thermodynamics by construction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports transferable complex-fluid models for CFD across deformation protocols and flow geometries without prescribing phenomenological constitutive equations.
method: Embed GENERIC thermodynamics in neural constitutive discovery.
Represent polymer microstructure in the conformation tensor’s intrinsic eigenspace.
Combine shear, extensional, and mixed-flow data to learn a shared constitutive model.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports validation against high-fidelity simulations, including constitutive reconstruction and flow-field prediction in previously unseen geometries, but provides no quantitative errors.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond the sampled microstructural states remains to be established; thermodynamic admissibility alone does not guarantee predictive accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: A GENERIC-Informed Neural Network for Generative Rheology

title: High-fidelity Three-Dimensional Flow Field Reconstruction Driven by Turbulent Fluid Dynamics
authors: Hanlin Kong, Jianan Wei, Yuntian Chen, Yujia Wang, Wenguan Wang
abstract: High-fidelity three-dimensional turbulent flow fields are essential for scientific and engineering analyses, yet obtaining them through direct numerical simulation or high-resolution measurements remains expensive. Super-resolution reconstruction from coarse-grained data therefore offers a promising alternative, but remains fundamentally challenging because fine-scale structures are intrinsically three-dimensional and dynamically coupled across scales. Existing data-driven approaches still struggle to recover multiscale volumetric structures and their coherent temporal evolution. To address these limitations, we propose a turbulence-aware framework for time-resolved three-dimensional flow reconstruction. The framework couples a multiscale neural operator, designed to recover volumetric structures, with a state space model to promote temporal consistency in the reconstructed dynamics. In addition, Navier-Stokes residuals are incorporated as soft constraints to regularize the reconstruction toward physically plausible dynamics. A mixture-of-experts mechanism is also introduced to support unsupervised adaptation to unknown coarse-graining. Across evaluations on canonical turbulent systems and atmospheric reanalysis data, the proposed framework reduces reconstruction errors relative to learning-based and classical baselines, while better preserving multiscale spatial structure and coherent temporal evolution. These results validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in reconstructing high-fidelity three-dimensional flow fields from coarse-grained data.

infographic.key_insight: A turbulence-aware AI framework reconstructs time-resolved 3D flow fields from coarse data while better preserving multiscale structures and temporal coherence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could reduce reliance on costly high-resolution simulations or measurements when detailed turbulent flow fields are needed for engineering analysis.
method: Combine a multiscale neural operator for volumetric reconstruction with a state space model for temporal consistency.
Use Navier–Stokes residuals as soft constraints to encourage physically plausible dynamics.
Introduce a mixture-of-experts mechanism for unsupervised adaptation to unknown coarse-graining.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations on canonical turbulent systems and atmospheric reanalysis data report lower reconstruction errors than learning-based and classical baselines, though the abstract provides no numerical gains.
infographic.watch_item: Soft physics constraints do not guarantee physical consistency; reconstructed fine-scale dynamics require validation before engineering use.
infographic.paper_title: High-fidelity Three-Dimensional Flow Field Reconstruction Driven by Turbulent Fluid Dynamics

title: Interaction of Sustained Vortex Shedding with a Phononic Subsurface: Effect of Positioning and Resonant Characteristics
authors: Sangwon Park, Vinod Ramakrishnan, Arturo Machado Burgos, Andres Goza, Kathryn H. Matlack
abstract: Phononic materials (PMs) have emerged as a promising candidate to passively and beneficially interact with unsteady flows. However, their fluid-structure interaction (FSI) with separated flows exhibiting sustained periodic vortex shedding remains completely unexplored. In this study, we use a high-fidelity immersed boundary method to investigate the strongly coupled, nonlinear FSI dynamics of vortex shedding from a fully separated flow over a flat plate, with an embedded PM subsurface (PSub) modeled as a grounded diatomic chain driving a compliant section on the flat plate. We probe the dependence of the coupled system dynamics on two parameters: (1) the PSub chordwise position, which sets its spatial relationship to the flow structure, and (2) the rate of growth of the resonant displacement amplitude of a PSub, a behavioral parameter identified as a key driving parameter in PSub interaction with latent vortex shedding in prior work. Simulation results show that these two parameters drive clear and systematic changes to the limit-cycle vortex shedding. The PSub chordwise position determines the limit cycle PM-FSI dynamics, which can be classified into four distinct regimes as a function of position, ranging from substantial amplification to strong attenuation of lift and drag oscillation amplitudes in the limit cycle. Results reveal a configuration that reduces lift oscillation amplitude by over 30% and drag oscillation amplitude by over 50% with less than 0.5% change in mean lift and drag. Displacement amplitude envelope primarily governs transient responsiveness toward the limit cycle, where its influence also depends on the chordwise position. We analyze characteristic frequencies, the phase relationship between PSub displacement and lift, and unsteady and mean flow fields of the vortex-shedding process to explain mechanisms by which the PM modifies the flow.

infographic.key_insight: Positioning a phononic subsurface beneath a separated flat-plate flow can either amplify or attenuate sustained vortex shedding, with one configuration substantially reducing force oscillations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Passive phononic subsurfaces could reduce unsteady aerodynamic loads while largely preserving mean lift and drag.
method: Simulated strongly coupled fluid–structure interaction using a high-fidelity immersed boundary method.
Modeled the subsurface as a grounded diatomic chain driving a compliant plate section.
Varied chordwise position and resonant displacement-amplitude growth; analyzed frequencies, phase relationships, and flow fields.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations identified four position-dependent limit-cycle regimes and a configuration reducing lift oscillation amplitude by over 30% and drag oscillation amplitude by over 50%, with less than 0.5% change in mean lift and drag.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is position-sensitive, and the abstract reports numerical results rather than experimental validation.
infographic.paper_title: Interaction of Sustained Vortex Shedding with a Phononic Subsurface: Effect of Positioning and Resonant Characteristics

title: Hurricane Laura-induced loads on wind turbines -- Part I: High-fidelity modeling and sensitivity to turbulent inflow conditions
authors: Miguel Sanchez-Gomez, Lucas Carmo, Matthew Churchfield, Jason Jonkman, Walter Musial
abstract: Tropical cyclones can produce extreme winds in the lowest portion of the boundary layer, posing high risks to critical energy infrastructure, including wind energy systems. This study evaluates the dynamic response of an idling wind turbine to turbulent inflow generated during the passage of a hurricane. We performed large-eddy simulations of Hurricane Laura (2020) at several grid resolutions -- coarse $(Δx=55.55\,{\rm m})$, intermediate $(Δx=25\,{\rm m})$, and fine $(Δx=10\,{\rm m})$ -- to investigate differences in mean flow characteristics and turbulence structures as the hurricane progresses across a virtual wind turbine location. The large-eddy simulation data served as direct inflow conditions for aeroelastic simulations to assess the turbine's response. Our results reveal significant differences in the mean wind and turbulent flow structures between the grid resolutions, leading to distinct impacts on the wind turbine's aeroelastic behavior. These findings emphasize the need for high-resolution inflow information to better predict extreme loads and inform the design of wind turbines in regions frequently affected by tropical cyclones. As a continuation of this work, Part II of this study will evaluate the turbine's response from different locations relative to the storm's trajectory and compare it with current wind turbine design practices.

infographic.key_insight: LES grid resolution changes predicted hurricane winds and turbulence, producing distinct aeroelastic responses in an idling wind turbine.
infographic.engineering_relevance: High-resolution hurricane inflow information can improve extreme-load prediction and support wind turbine design in cyclone-prone regions.
method: Simulate Hurricane Laura (2020) using large-eddy simulation.
Compare grid spacings of 55.55 m, 25 m, and 10 m.
Use LES inflow directly in aeroelastic simulations of an idling turbine.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three grid resolutions, the simulations showed significant differences in mean winds and turbulence structures that affected turbine response.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no quantitative load differences or validation against measurements, and comparisons across storm-relative locations are deferred to Part II.
infographic.paper_title: Hurricane Laura-induced loads on wind turbines -- Part I: High-fidelity modeling and sensitivity to turbulent inflow conditions

title: Effects of Spanwise Curvature on Hypersonic Boundary Layer Transition in Görtler-driven Flows
authors: Andrew Welter, Ngoc Cuong Nguyen, Nicholas Webber, Mark Gragston, Jaime Peraire, Wesley Harris
abstract: The influence of spanwise convex curvature on hypersonic boundary-layer transition over a streamwise-concave surface is investigated using direct numerical simulation and Mach 7 experiments. Smooth doubly curved geometries with fixed streamwise concavity and increasing spanwise convex curvature isolate the effects of three-dimensional wall curvature on a centrifugally unstable boundary layer. Increasing spanwise curvature delays transition while preserving a Gortler-dominated route to breakdown. As spanwise curvature increases, the boundary layer thins, reducing the effective Görtler number and weakening centrifugal amplification of streamwise vortices. Consequently, growth of the primary Görtler instability is reduced, vortical structures remain closer to the wall, and secondary instability and turbulent breakdown shift downstream. Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition confirms that low-frequency vortical dynamics remain dominant in controlling transition, with sinuous secondary instability of Görtler vortices providing the principal route to breakdown. Meanwhile, boundary-layer thinning modifies acoustic instability dynamics: the second Mack mode shifts to higher frequencies and higher-frequency supersonic disturbances become increasingly prominent near breakdown as spanwise curvature increases. These acoustic disturbances remain subdominant and do not replace the Görtler-sinuous mechanism as the primary transition pathway. Numerical and experimental results exhibit consistent trends in transition location, thermal-streak organisation and disturbance evolution, supporting a common physical interpretation. These findings demonstrate that spanwise convex curvature stabilises hypersonic Görtler-dominated boundary layers, primarily by suppressing centrifugal amplification and delaying secondary instability, while leaving the transition pathway qualitatively unchanged.

infographic.key_insight: Increasing spanwise convex curvature delays hypersonic boundary-layer transition by weakening centrifugal amplification while preserving the dominant Görtler–sinuous breakdown pathway.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Spanwise curvature offers a potential geometry-based lever for delaying transition and managing surface heating in hypersonic designs.
method: Direct numerical simulation and Mach 7 experiments.
Smooth doubly curved surfaces with fixed streamwise concavity and increasing spanwise convex curvature.
Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition to identify dominant disturbance dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations and experiments show consistent trends in transition location, thermal-streak organisation and disturbance evolution, with greater spanwise curvature delaying breakdown.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify transition-delay magnitude or establish applicability beyond the tested geometries and flow conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Effects of Spanwise Curvature on Hypersonic Boundary Layer Transition in Görtler-driven Flows

title: How the elastic axis folds the transonic flutter boundary: shock energy transfer and conformally calibrated active learning
authors: Ashray Saxena, Sharad Shrivastava
abstract: Isogai's case A, a pitch-plunge aerofoil whose elastic axis lies half a chord ahead of the leading edge, has a folded transonic flutter boundary in inviscid flow: near the bottom of the transonic dip several flutter speeds coexist at one Mach number. We map this boundary, and the family obtained by moving the elastic axis, with coupled unsteady Euler simulations, a Gaussian-process surrogate of the damping coefficient trained by batch active learning, and split conformal prediction on independent random simulations, which turns the surrogate into stability calls with a distribution-free error rate. Three failure modes of time-domain damping labels that leave no trace in the residuals are documented, and the half-degree mean incidence left by the common one-degree start is shown to raise the flutter speed at the dip by 2.8%, more than any numerical setting. With 80 simulations the learned case A boundary labels 64 of 65 independent runs correctly, and calibrated calls are wrong in at most 1.6% of cases. Over Mach number, elastic axis and flutter speed index, 193 simulations and 40 calibration runs show that the fold exists only for elastic axes more than about 0.4 chord ahead of the leading edge; it closes between 0.39 and 0.33 chord ahead, on two meshes. Chordwise energy budgets, closed against the solver loads and the growth rate within a few per cent, explain the boundary. The lower branch is crossed through the reduced frequency at unchanged shock phase. On the upper branch the shock is pinned at the trailing edge, and moving the elastic axis aft brings the pivot of the flutter mode towards the section, so that the damping of the supersonic surface falls faster than the residual shock input and the fold closes.

infographic.key_insight: Moving the elastic axis aft closes the folded transonic flutter boundary by reducing supersonic-surface damping faster than the residual shock energy input.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Elastic-axis placement can determine whether multiple flutter-speed thresholds coexist at one Mach number, complicating aeroelastic stability assessment.
method: Coupled unsteady Euler simulations of a pitch–plunge aerofoil with varying elastic-axis position.
Batch active learning of a Gaussian-process damping surrogate, calibrated using independent split conformal prediction.
Chordwise energy budgets to explain shock-driven energy transfer and fold closure.
infographic.evidence_signal: With 80 simulations, the case A model correctly labeled 64 of 65 independent runs; a broader study using 193 simulations and 40 calibration runs placed fold closure between 0.39 and 0.33 chord ahead of the leading edge on two meshes.
infographic.watch_item: Results concern inviscid flow, and time-domain damping labels require careful checks: the common one-degree start left a mean incidence that raised dip flutter speed by 2.8%.
infographic.paper_title: How the elastic axis folds the transonic flutter boundary: shock energy transfer and conformally calibrated active learning

title: Component-wise outer similarity of turbulent boundary layers with strong adverse-pressure gradient
authors: Yu-Xuan Shi, Mingze Ma, Xi Chen
abstract: The adverse-pressure-gradient (APG) effect challenges the classical scaling of turbulent boundary layers (TBLs) over a flat plate, and it remains unclear whether outer-layer similarity holds across a wide range of APG strengths.We assemble a benchmark comprising the present direct numerical simulation of a suction--blowing-induced separation bubble and published profiles, spanning Clauser parameters $β_e=0.04$--$180$ and Reynolds numbers $Re_θ=530$--$19000$. Across this broad $(β_e,Re_θ)$ parameter range, existing APG normalizations do not simultaneously collapse the two mean-velocity defects and four Reynolds-stress components, leaving open whether outer similarity persists. Instead of defining new scalings, we normalize each quantity by its value at a common location $y_s$. Results are shown using $y_s=0.5δ$, beyond the outer stress peaks. For each of the six quantities, the normalized profiles exhibit a common outer shape across the conditions, with collapse emerging for $y/δ\gtrsim0.2$ for the velocity defects and $y/δ\gtrsim0.4$ for the Reynolds stresses. The collapse-error analysis shows that outer self-similarity is retained over a broad range of $y_s$ within the outer region and is not restricted to $y_s=0.5δ$. Furthermore, explicit expressions are provided for the normalized outer profiles. These results support component-wise outer similarity under strong APGs and provide compact references for APG turbulence-model assessment and conditional profile reconstruction.

infographic.key_insight: Under strong adverse pressure gradients, turbulent boundary layers retain component-wise outer similarity when each velocity defect or Reynolds stress is normalized by its own value at a shared outer-layer location.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Compact outer-profile expressions offer references for assessing APG turbulence models and reconstructing profiles when component amplitudes are known.
method: Combine separation-bubble DNS with published turbulent-boundary-layer profiles.
Normalize two mean-velocity defects and four Reynolds stresses by their respective values at a common location, illustrated at y_s = 0.5δ.
Assess profile collapse across conditions and test sensitivity to the normalization location.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across β_e = 0.04–180 and Re_θ = 530–19,000, collapse emerges at y/δ ≳ 0.2 for velocity defects and ≳ 0.4 for Reynolds stresses, and persists over a broad range of outer normalization locations.
infographic.watch_item: The similarity is component-wise and outer-layer-specific; reconstruction still requires each quantity’s value at the chosen normalization location.
infographic.paper_title: Component-wise outer similarity of turbulent boundary layers with strong adverse-pressure gradient

title: PINN-LPCDD: Physics-Informed Neural Network with Learnable and Physically Consistent Domain Decomposition for Compressible Multi-Medium Flows
authors: Weiheng Zeng, Hao Wang, Jiaxin Zhu, Kun Wang, Tiegang Liu, Chengliang Feng
abstract: The physics-informed neural network (PINN) faces significant challenges when solving compressible multi-medium flows, including the inability to locate interface positions, poor approximation of discontinuities, and difficulty in handling high-pressure-ratio problems between media with large stiffness differences. To address these issues, we propose PINN with Learnable and Physically Consistent Domain Decomposition (PINN-LPCDD), a framework that incorporates the sharp interface method (SIM) into PINNs for solving compressible multi-medium flows. Firstly, we design separate sub-networks for each medium with learnable parameters to automatically learn interface positions, so that the domain decomposition is physically consistent, and the contact discontinuity at the interface is naturally sharp. Secondly, the Euler equations with artificial viscosity are solved to enhance robustness when handling problems involving shock waves. Lastly, the scaling invariance of the Euler equations is exploited to facilitate the solution of high pressure ratio problems. Numerical experiments on air-air, air-helium, air-water, and air-R22 problems demonstrate the acceptable accuracy of the proposed method in simulating multi-medium flows.

infographic.key_insight: PINN-LPCDD learns physically consistent interfaces between media, enabling sharp contact discontinuities in compressible multi-medium flow simulations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets shock-driven flows involving large pressure ratios and media with strongly differing stiffness.
method: Use separate neural networks for each medium and learn interface positions through sharp-interface domain decomposition.
Solve Euler equations with artificial viscosity to improve robustness around shock waves.
Exploit Euler-equation scaling invariance to handle high pressure ratios.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments on air–air, air–helium, air–water, and air–R22 problems report acceptable accuracy, without quantitative metrics in the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: Sensitivity to artificial-viscosity settings and interface-training choices should be checked; the abstract does not establish computational efficiency.
infographic.paper_title: PINN-LPCDD: Physics-Informed Neural Network with Learnable and Physically Consistent Domain Decomposition for Compressible Multi-Medium Flows

title: Pair-exchange dynamics of magnetohydrodynamic turbulence
authors: Jean-Mathieu Teissier, Wolf-Christian Müller
abstract: Nonlinear interactions in incompressible magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) and Navier-Stokes turbulence involve three spatial fluctuations conservatively exchanging, e.g., energy. The mathematical structure of a triad interaction does not allow to unambigously determine the specific contribution of each of the participating fluctuations to the resulting exchanges. Presently, only additional assumptions allow for the deconstruction of triad interactions into a sum of pair exchanges. This work proves that in incompressible MHD the simultaneous nonlinear transfer of cross-helicity sufficiently constrains the triad dynamics such that a mathematically unique pair-exchange representation of nonlinear energy and cross-helicity transfer is possible.

infographic.key_insight: Simultaneous cross-helicity transfer uniquely determines pairwise energy and cross-helicity exchanges within nonlinear triads in incompressible MHD turbulence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This result offers a rigorous basis for interpreting energy-transfer pathways in incompressible MHD simulations relevant to conducting-fluid and plasma flows.
method: Analyze conservative nonlinear exchanges among three interacting spatial fluctuations.
Use simultaneous cross-helicity transfer to constrain triad dynamics.
Prove uniqueness of the pair-exchange representation for energy and cross-helicity transfer.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a mathematical uniqueness proof, but no numerical benchmarks, experimental data, or AI-based evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: The result is established for incompressible MHD; applicability to compressible flows or Navier–Stokes turbulence is not demonstrated in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Pair-exchange dynamics of magnetohydrodynamic turbulence

title: Hydrodynamics and propulsive efficiency of stern-sculling propulsion
authors: Gildas Roudaut, Benoit Augier, Marc Rabaud
abstract: Stern-sculling is a traditional form of human-powered boat propulsion in which a single oar is oscillated laterally at the stern. In this study, we investigate this propulsion technique from a hydrodynamic perspective by continuously measuring the oar kinematics, the boat motion, and the forces acting on the oar across a broad range of boat speeds. During the lateral strokes, lift serves as the main propulsive force, whereas during the backward strokes, propulsion is primarily associated with added-mass effects. These measurements allow us to determine the propulsive efficiency as a function of boat speed. The efficiency peaks at approximately 65\% at an intermediate speed and then decreases progressively to approximately 25\% at higher speeds. These results provide insight into the hydrodynamic mechanisms governing this traditional mode of propulsion and highlight the effectiveness of stern-sculling at moderate speeds.

infographic.key_insight: Stern-sculling propulsion relies mainly on lift during lateral strokes and added-mass effects during backward strokes, with peak efficiency near 65% at intermediate boat speed.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The findings can inform oscillating-oar propulsion design and operating speeds for efficient human-powered boats.
method: Continuously measure oar kinematics and boat motion.
Measure forces acting on the oar across a broad range of boat speeds.
Determine propulsive efficiency as a function of boat speed.
infographic.evidence_signal: Measurements show efficiency peaking at approximately 65% at intermediate speed and declining to approximately 25% at higher speeds.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports experimental measurements, not an AI or CFD surrogate, and does not establish generalizability across oar geometries or boat designs.
infographic.paper_title: Hydrodynamics and propulsive efficiency of stern-sculling propulsion

title: SCP-FTLE and SCP-FSLE: High-performance finite-time and finite-size Lyapunov-exponent computations for CPUs and GPUs
authors: Huanxia Wei, Mengqi Zhang
abstract: Finite-time and finite-size Lyapunov exponents (FTLE and FSLE) characterise material stretching and transport barriers over prescribed time intervals and separation scales, but their evaluation from three-dimensional velocity sequences requires large computational costs. We introduce SCP-FTLE and SCP-FSLE, two modules of StreamCenter+ for CPU- and GPU-accelerated Lagrangian analysis. The modules support structured and native unstructured meshes, selectable integration and interpolation schemes, and graphical and command-line workflows. Rolling snapshot reuse, memory-bounded FTLE batching, device-resident trajectory state and active-set FSLE advancement reduce data movement and redundant computation, achieving the state-of-the-art (SOTA) computational performance among peer packages. For a billion-seed benchmark, strong-scaling efficiencies on 32 GPUs reach 86.3% for FTLE and 95.2% for FSLE. FTLE is verified with published steady and unsteady Arnold-Beltrami-Childress (ABC) flows and stationary concentrated vortex model (SCVM), while FSLE is verified in linear stretching and rotational shear flows. As examples, applications reveal the spanwise reorganisation of stretching layers in a shear-thinning lid-driven cavity, and resolve three-dimensional stretching structures associated with contrasting tracer dispersion around an urban building canopy at NUS campus. These results demonstrate a scalable workflow in large-scale Lagrangian diagnostics and analysis of flow data.

infographic.key_insight: SCP-FTLE and SCP-FSLE accelerate three-dimensional material-stretching and transport-barrier analysis on CPUs and GPUs while scaling efficiently to a billion seeds.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The modules enable large-scale flow-transport diagnostics, including mixing in shear-thinning cavity flows and tracer dispersion around urban buildings.
method: Support structured and native unstructured meshes with selectable integration and interpolation schemes.
Reduce data movement through rolling snapshot reuse, memory-bounded FTLE batching and device-resident trajectory state.
Use active-set FSLE advancement to reduce redundant computation.
infographic.evidence_signal: For a billion-seed benchmark, 32-GPU strong-scaling efficiencies reach 86.3% for FTLE and 95.2% for FSLE; verification uses ABC and SCVM flows for FTLE and linear stretching and rotational shear flows for FSLE.
infographic.watch_item: Performance and accuracy on new datasets should be checked against available memory, mesh characteristics and integration/interpolation choices.
infographic.paper_title: SCP-FTLE and SCP-FSLE: High-performance finite-time and finite-size Lyapunov-exponent computations for CPUs and GPUs

title: Magnetic flux ring splitting near a Navier-Stokes singularity
authors: Antti J. Niemi
abstract: OpenAI reports a forced Navier-Stokes flow that becomes singular in finite time, raising the question of its physical consequences. Magnetic reconnection offers a test through the splitting and merging of flux structures. We use resistive magnetohydrodynamics to simulate a magnetic ring driven by an imposed, regularized flow that reproduces the geometry and scaling of the collapsing core. At the nominal singular time, we remove the imposed drive and allow the system to evolve freely. Reconnections before and after release split the ring into two or more daughter rings through bifurcations of the poloidal flux function, with Lorentz feedback selecting the bifurcation type. Unequal winding by the swirl above and below the midplane produces asymmetric toroidal magnetic stresses, unfolding the kinematic pitchfork-like transition into a fold. For single-island splits, the cusp normal form predicts the asymmetry of the daughter rings without adjustable parameters. Three-dimensional simulations retain the splits and merger, confirming that approach to hydrodynamic blow-up can trigger magnetic restructuring.

infographic.key_insight: A regularized flow approaching a proposed Navier–Stokes singularity can trigger magnetic reconnection that splits a flux ring into daughter rings.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results connect rapidly collapsing flow structures to magnetic topology changes, informing the modeling of strongly driven conducting fluids and plasmas.
method: Simulate a magnetic ring with resistive magnetohydrodynamics under an imposed, regularized collapsing flow.
Remove the imposed drive at the nominal singular time and track subsequent reconnection.
Analyze poloidal-flux bifurcations and Lorentz feedback, with three-dimensional simulations checking persistence.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports parameter-free cusp predictions of daughter-ring asymmetry for single-island splits, while three-dimensional simulations retain splitting and merger.
infographic.watch_item: The imposed flow is regularized, so these simulations do not establish a Navier–Stokes singularity or its consequences in an unregularized physical system.
infographic.paper_title: Magnetic flux ring splitting near a Navier-Stokes singularity

title: Some generalizations of the tornado model
authors: S. N. Artekha
abstract: A possible mechanism of tornado generation is associated with the Schwarzschild criterion for convective instability. The supercooled cloud-air mixture near the axis starts to descend and, due to the super adiabatic temperature gradient, the overheated near-surface air mass rises. The complete system of equations for full model includes equations for the stream function, for the azimuthal velocity component, and for the change in density. The refined model considers rotating convection within the framework of ideal hydrodynamics. The simplest model uses a separate equation for the stream function and can be applied to the initial stage of vortex generation. Within the framework of the simplest model, an analytical solution is combined from 8 linear dependencies by height. Rotation increases due to the conservation of angular momentum. Within the framework of the refined model, some unidirectional differential rotation arises, but it depends on boundary conditions (can be local). The full model studies the tornado development as rotating convection from the very beginning to the quasi-stationary stage. Velocity components increase in a coordinated manner. Two cases are considered: a single whirlwind and a two-eyed tornado. Radial flows converge towards the central part of the tornado near the earth surface, and there is an outflow from the "wall" to the axis and to the periphery near the top of the tornado. The maximum vertical velocity component is achieved at a certain radial distance at a certain height. The maximum azimuthal velocity component is achieved in the tornado "wall". Tornado generation criteria are discussed.

infographic.key_insight: A hierarchy of ideal-hydrodynamic models describes tornado formation as rotating convection driven by thermal instability, with coordinated growth of velocity components.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The models offer a theoretical framework for investigating vortex initiation, near-surface inflow, and peak wind locations in tornado-like flows.
method: Link convective onset to the Schwarzschild instability criterion.
Develop simplest, refined, and full models coupling stream function, azimuthal velocity, and density change at increasing levels of complexity.
Construct an analytical solution for the simplest model and examine single-whirlwind and two-eyed tornado configurations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical modeling and predicted flow structures, but provides no quantitative validation against observations or experiments.
infographic.watch_item: Ideal-hydrodynamic assumptions and boundary-condition-sensitive rotation may limit applicability to real atmospheric tornadoes.
infographic.paper_title: Some generalizations of the tornado model

title: Wake effects in a 100 GW North Sea offshore wind scenario: a model intercomparison under year-round weather conditions
authors: Jhon J. Quiñones, Diego Siguenza-Alvarado, Peter Baas, Pim Van Dorp, Majid Bastankhah, Remco A. Verzijlbergh
abstract: Large-scale offshore wind development will intensify wake interactions between wind farm clusters in the North Sea, increasing uncertainty in regional energy estimates. We assess HARMONIE-AROME mesoscale simulations, ASPIRE large-eddy simulations (LES), and three engineering wake models based on Jensen, Bastankhah Gaussian, and TurbOPark formulations for a 100.7 GW 2050 offshore wind scenario. We find that LES and mesoscale simulations accurately represent observed local free-stream wind conditions. Moreover, all engineering wake models predict higher mean wind speeds than LES in every month, with biases reaching 0.60-0.70 m/s at 10-40 km downstream. These differences also vary systematically with atmospheric regime: the Bastankhah Gaussian model remains positively biased across wind speed and stability conditions, whereas Jensen and TurbOPark shift from underprediction in unstable and near-neutral conditions to overprediction in stable conditions at 8-12 m/s. These results show that agreement in annual capacity factor can conceal substantial differences across space, time, and atmospheric regime, highlighting the importance of including sensitivity to model formulation in regional wind energy assessments.

infographic.key_insight: Agreement in annual capacity factor can mask substantial differences in predicted offshore wind wakes across locations, seasons, and atmospheric regimes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Regional wind-energy assessments should account for wake-model sensitivity when estimating production from a 100.7 GW North Sea build-out.
method: Evaluate a 2050 offshore wind scenario under year-round weather conditions.
Compare HARMONIE-AROME mesoscale simulations, ASPIRE large-eddy simulations, and three engineering wake models.
Assess wake predictions across downstream distance, wind speed, and atmospheric stability.
infographic.evidence_signal: LES and mesoscale simulations accurately represent observed local free-stream winds, while all three engineering models predict higher monthly mean wind speeds than LES, with biases reaching 0.60–0.70 m/s at 10–40 km downstream.
infographic.watch_item: Validation against local free-stream observations does not establish wake accuracy across the full region; engineering-model biases also depend on atmospheric regime.
infographic.paper_title: Wake effects in a 100 GW North Sea offshore wind scenario: a model intercomparison under year-round weather conditions

title: Effect of leading edge geometry on aerodynamic performance of a flat plate
authors: Intesaaf Ashraf, Hamid Hassan Khan, Majid Hassan Khan
abstract: Flow separation around flat plate is influenced by the thickness and leading edge geometry, which creates the shear stresses and pressure distribution manifesting into unsteady aerodynamic forces. Leading edge geometries have been widely reported but the influence of leading edge curvature at low Reynolds numbers (Re) have found less attention. The present study uses two dimensional numerical simulation to investigate the effect of a hemispherical curvature (protuberance) at the leading edge and reports how vortex shedding, shedding frequencies and aerodynamic forces are affected over a range of angles of attack ($0^\circ \leq α\leq 25^\circ$) at Re = 1000. Thicker vortical regions are formed near the plate with curvature at the leading edge. Onset of shedding is noted at angle of attack of $5^\circ$ for the plate with curvature at the leading edge and it gets delayed for simple flat plate. The temporal force coefficients on the plates show multiple frequencies at higher angles of attack. The plate with curvature at the leading edge has a glide ratio of 1 at $0^\circ$ angle of attack and has equivalent glide ratio to that of simple flat plate at higher angles of attack. The simple flat plate has better glide ratios at moderate angles of attack like $5^\circ, 10^\circ$ and $15^\circ$. The results will help in making engineering informed design decisions for smaller unmanned aerial/aquatic vehicles cruising at low Reynolds numbers.

infographic.key_insight: At Re = 1000, a hemispherical leading-edge protuberance produces thicker vortical regions and shedding onset at 5°, while a simple flat plate achieves better glide ratios at 5°, 10°, and 15°.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Leading-edge geometry can guide aerodynamic design choices for small unmanned aerial or aquatic vehicles operating at low Reynolds numbers.
method: Two-dimensional numerical flow simulations at Re = 1000.
Compared a simple flat plate with a plate featuring a hemispherical leading-edge protuberance.
Examined vortex shedding, frequencies, and aerodynamic forces over angles of attack from 0° to 25°.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations show multiple force-coefficient frequencies at higher angles of attack and comparable glide ratios between the two geometries at higher angles.
infographic.watch_item: Results are limited to two-dimensional simulations at one Reynolds number; three-dimensional and experimental validation would be needed before vehicle-scale application.
infographic.paper_title: Effect of leading edge geometry on aerodynamic performance of a flat plate

title: Extreme-Scale Super-Resolution of Homogeneous Turbulence from a Single Realization
authors: Arth Sojitra, Muhammad Abid, Omer San
abstract: Homogeneous turbulent flows exhibit recurring multiscale structures across spatially separated regions, suggesting that a single flow realization may contain sufficient information to learn representations of unresolved scales. We investigate this hypothesis through an extreme super-resolution framework in which a wide-activation deep super-resolution (WDSR) network is trained exclusively on overlapping patches extracted from a single high-resolution turbulent realization. Previously unseen flow fields are reconstructed through patchwise prediction followed by Hann-window-weighted overlap-add assembly. The framework is evaluated for two-dimensional homogeneous isotropic turbulence at super-resolution factors of x32 and x64, representing severe spatial under-resolution. Despite the limited training data, the proposed approach reconstructs coherent vortical structures and recovers fine-scale features more accurately than conventional interpolation. Spectral and statistical analyses further demonstrate improved recovery of high-wavenumber energy content and multiscale flow characteristics. To assess the effectiveness of exploiting internal spatial information, we compare the proposed framework against WDSR models trained on 1, 25, 50, and 100 complete high-resolution snapshots without patch extraction. This comparison distinguishes the benefits of localized learning from those associated with increasing the number of training realizations. The results demonstrate that exploiting spatial redundancy within a single turbulent realization enables accurate reconstruction of previously unseen flow fields, even under extreme spatial under-resolution. These findings establish single-realization patch-based learning as a promising data-efficient approach for turbulent super-resolution when high-resolution training data are scarce.

infographic.key_insight: Learning from overlapping patches of a single turbulent realization enables extreme ×32 and ×64 super-resolution of previously unseen flow fields.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This data-efficient approach could help reconstruct under-resolved turbulent flows when high-resolution training data are scarce.
method: Train a wide-activation deep super-resolution (WDSR) network on overlapping patches from one high-resolution realization.
Predict unseen fields patchwise and assemble them using Hann-window-weighted overlap-add.
Compare against interpolation and WDSR models trained on 1, 25, 50, or 100 complete snapshots.
infographic.evidence_signal: In two-dimensional homogeneous isotropic turbulence at ×32 and ×64, the abstract reports improved vortical structures, fine-scale features, and high-wavenumber energy recovery relative to interpolation.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to two-dimensional homogeneous isotropic turbulence; transfer to three-dimensional or more complex engineering flows remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Extreme-Scale Super-Resolution of Homogeneous Turbulence from a Single Realization

title: eMOOD: Entropy-Based Multidimensional Optimal Order Detection for High-Order Shock-Capturing Finite-Volume Schemes
authors: Michał Umiński, Panagiotis Tsoutsanis, Ahmed A Sheikh Al-Shabab, Alan S. Dawes
abstract: We present eMOOD, an entropy-guided evolution of the Multidimensional Optimal Order Detection (MOOD) framework for high-order finite-volume methods on unstructured meshes. A novel troubled-cell indicator based on numerical entropy production replaces the classical relaxed discrete maximum principle. Using entropy generation as a physically motivated measure of non-smoothness, the detector targets shocks, contact discontinuities and under-resolved flow features with a compact stencil. Compared with conventional MOOD detection, eMOOD reduces flagged cells by up to 75%, improving efficiency and reducing memory-access overhead. The detector is used within both the classical MOOD cascade of progressively reduced-order schemes and a novel MOOD-CWENO hybrid, which retains inexpensive linear reconstruction in smooth regions and activates nonlinear high-order reconstruction only where needed. Implemented in the open-source parallel solver UCNS3D, the methodology is assessed on the Shu-Osher shock-entropy-wave interaction, double Mach reflection, supersonic forward-facing step, shock-helium-bubble interaction and triple material point problems. These benchmarks encompass strong shock interactions, shock-induced instabilities, multi-material interfaces and vortex-dominated flows, testing robustness, shock capturing and accuracy on unstructured meshes. Results show that eMOOD preserves the accuracy and robustness of reference CWENO and MOOD formulations while achieving speed-ups of up to 20% without loss of solution quality. Its compact detection stencil, reduced memory footprint and improved localisation offer a more scalable and efficient framework for massively parallel high-order compressible-flow simulations. infographic.key_insight: eMOOD uses numerical entropy production to localise troubled cells, reducing flagged cells by up to 75% while preserving high-order shock-capturing accuracy and robustness.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach can accelerate compressible and multi-material flow simulations on unstructured meshes, with reported speed-ups of up to 20%.
method: Replace relaxed discrete maximum-principle detection with a compact entropy-production indicator.
Apply detection within a reduced-order MOOD cascade or a MOOD-CWENO hybrid that activates nonlinear reconstruction only where needed.
Implement and evaluate the method in the open-source parallel solver UCNS3D.
infographic.evidence_signal: Five benchmarks, including Shu–Osher interaction, double Mach reflection and shock–helium-bubble interaction, test shock capturing, instabilities and multi-material interfaces against reference CWENO and MOOD formulations.
infographic.watch_item: The reported gains are benchmark-dependent; the abstract does not establish performance across broader flow regimes or at massive parallel scale.
infographic.paper_title: eMOOD: Entropy-Based Multidimensional Optimal Order Detection for High-Order Shock-Capturing Finite-Volume Schemes
